full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll start off telling you what we’re doing,

Subject:	OK, yeah, sure.

Interviewer:	It’s a big project looking at women engineering student’s experiences of their industrial placement. Are you going on placement?

Subject:	Yeah, I hope so.

Interviewer:	We are actually interviewing people who aren’t going on the placement as well to compare their views, but we’re looking at student placements to see what effect that has on your career intentions and things like that. We want to know what things you’re expecting to get out of your placement and your experiences in education and things like that. Are you doing the civil engineering course?

Subject:	Yeah I am –a B Eng.

Interviewer:	Did you do ‘A’ levels?

Subject:	I did yeah.

Interviewer:	What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did physics, chemistry, maths, and surprisingly Chinese.

Interviewer:	What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	I went to a – just a local yeah high school and college type.

Interviewer:	It wasn’t an all girls school or anything like that?

Subject:	No, no.

Interviewer:	Right, OK. Have you had any other work experience?

Subject:	Erm, I haven’t yet, apart from some part-time.

Interviewer:	Nothing in the engineering industry?

Subject:	No, no.

Interviewer:	OK, What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers?

Subject:	No, my dad’s a fireman – my mum’s just – she runs a café.

Interviewer:	Oh right, I’m going to ask you a little bit now about why you decided to study engineering (OK) so when and why do you think that you did decide to…?

Subject:	When? I think I first started to think about engineering when I was first choosing – I think towards the end of GCSE’s, ‘cos I realised I was a lot better at sciences and maths really, rather than some – you know – some subjects you’re not involved with them – a lot of reading, writing yeah? Yeah where it’s – yeah, I’ve got engineering skills. I started with er doing a chemistry degree. It went nowhere, yeah, so and then it just sort of – we confirmed that engineering would be good. Why choose civil engineering? I think it’s because of the physical scale of the project – I like to be involved – and I could have gone or the chemical or chemical engineering but erm, I – well in a way, I like of it – I liked all the architecture and stuff so I thought, it could be related. So I thought yeah, civil engineering would be best for me, in terms of engineering, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, so have your family been supportive of engineering?

Subject:	Er, yeah, yeah, they’re like ahh, you’re gonna be a professional (laughter) – yeah, hopefully one day.

Interviewer:	So they didn’t think you should be doing another subject?

Subject:	No, my parents are very open-minded.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much research into your career? Did you know any other engineers to speak to?

Subject:	Er, no I didn’t really but er my – well I did, actually, er if I said I didn’t I was lying because my uncle is a civil engineer, so he gave me sort of – I spoke to him because he’s in Hong Kong. I talked to him a couple of times and ask him why he decide to – you know – to do civil engineering – yeah. Before I contacted him, I thought quite similar material – architectural study and then I found the other aero spectrum – yeah, I think civil engineering suit me the best.

Interviewer:	Did you always know that you wanted to do the sandwich course?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK, any particular reason why you wanted to do that?

Subject:	Erm, I – well it appeared to me to be really good experience before I – you know – graduate or you know er before I go into it in the real world – yeah – so I started. It gives – I don’t know – if it’s true but I feel you probably stand a better chance, in terms of finding a graduate job when I finish on the…

Interviewer:	How did you decide to come to [this] University?

Subject:	How? It’s just the nearest because I’m from [town] – yeah. I don’t really go away from home, too far, ‘cos er I live with my younger brother. I still have to care for him and things like that. So, yeah, [this university] is really good. I’ve been here to visit friends a couple of times, and I really, really – the first time I got here I really, really like the campus and I think that’s one of the main attractions. Yeah

Interviewer:	OK, could you have gone to [name] University?

Subject:	Erm, well, I did my chemistry degree in [university]. And another thing is they don’t do civil engineering. If they did I would have considered it as well because I – well, yeah, ‘cos I didn’t really want to commute every day, because I don’t drive myself, yeah, but this was the nearest and I can get there.

Interviewer:	Do you get the train then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, when you decided to do engineering, did you realise it was so male-dominated?

Subject:	Well, I’ve always known ‘cos – well, obviously my uncle when he was in (?) – well she – well he – he warned me as well and I say, I’m going to go for it.

Interviewer:	Is the situation the same in Hong Kong then is it?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, it is yeah. I think it’s more so in Hong Kong than in England.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so – it’s good, it’s professional. It’s – I don’t see why not ‘cos obviously you – I mean you just get involved with the project. I – I personally don’t see why not because – or I don’t expect, you know, when we finish the degree, that you have to handle really heavy duty and that kind of thing, you know, in terms of shifting or that kind of thing. I – yes, so I don’t see any reason why not. If you enjoy maths and science then – those subjects, I don’t see why not, yes. 

Interviewer:	Why do you think there aren’t more women in engineering then?

Subject:	I think just traditions. Erm, but yeah that’s about it, I think and…

Interviewer:	Do you think maybe women don’t realise what it’s all about?

Subject:	Yes, because like when they think of engineering then they think of all the plumbing, you know, that kind of stuff. They don’t realise – I don’t think they actually know what engineering means. I think you know – most of the people would think of how do you fix an (oven?) or that kind of thing. Or how do you fix a car, you know? Like I said, not many girls are fond of cars and I think that’s why. They don’t realise. They’re so – there are so many types of engineering going on.

Interviewer:	How do you think that more women could be encouraged to do engineering then?

Subject:	Well, I think to start with er I think some kind of education or some talk could be good in like primary or – not – primary’s probably too young – secondary schools. 

Interviewer:	Yeah, people could go in and tell them what…

Subject:	Yeah, yeah tell them – well specially tell the girls – could tell the boys as well - remind the girls it’s not just a boys’ subject, you know, that kind of thing. I think – well yeah, it is like give them an idea at a young age rather than – well, as a sensible student they should sort of like have an idea of what they want to do at probably GCSE studies you know – yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, characteristic – I’m not sure ‘cos – well it’s very general I think you have to have this characteristic and also – ‘cos also if you want to do the choice in your career well – but civil engineering it’s probably – the workload, its much heavier than others – I don’t know because I haven’t done, you know, any other areas yet. Erm, 

Interviewer:	Do you think people doing chemistry and people doing civil engineering have different characteristics then?

Subject:	Well really I do, yeah. Erm doing – people doing like civil engineering, they’re very determined. They’re very determined in terms of where they want to end up being, like a few years or really what they want to do. Erm, yeah, erm quite strong minded and I think more ambitious as well.

Interviewer:	Do you think there’s a difference between women engineers and men engineers? Do you think they have different characteristics?

Subject:	Yeah, could be. Erm, I’m not sure other women but for myself, erm, from my point of view, I think women engineer they are – for a woman going into like engineering, I – or civil engineering, talking about that, they’re generally quite aggressive in term of what they want to achieve in their life, you know, and well ambitious – I should use the word. Not – yeah, but probably for men it’s just – yeah, one of the area I can succeed in, you know, that kind of thing. I could be wrong but I – I do feel that there is something like competition between female and the male in this – in the same industry. But being civil engineering, it’s so dominated by males. The female would think, if you can do it why can’t I do it? You know that kind of feeling.

Interviewer:	So you think that’s why the women are more ambitious probably? (yeah, yeah) Because they have to prove that basically?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of being a female engineer?

Subject:	Erm, it depends what kind of people do you meet, when you’re out there. If you meet some good, caring people, they are – ‘cos I had some – I had some interview with some employers when I was looking for a placement and they were all saying they tend to look after female, especially when they work on site but then again if you meet like some – I don’t know – some like more traditional thinking male you might – you know – probably have a hard time. Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, I’m going to ask you some things about your course so far. (Right OK) When you started doing the engineering course what did you expect from it, in terms of like the type of things you’ve been taught and the type of teaching, and maybe the gender proportions and anything really like that?

Subject:	Er, I suppose – basically my expectation so far, you know, all kinds of things – I’m accepted here and male only and all the calculations and stuff like that, yes.

Interviewer:	OK and what have been the best and the worst things about your course, so far?

Subject:	The best – er, I can’t think of anything (laughs). The best erm 

Interviewer:	It doesn’t have to be a specific thing, it might be like a general thing or…

Subject:	The lecturers are very nice and the whole department is very friendly and you do feel part of it, not just one of the students – yes. And the worst – the worst is – well the workload is a little bit heavier than I would have expected.

Interviewer:	It is?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Is it harder work or more work than you (had to do) in chemistry?

Subject:	Oh it’s a lot – yeah. I do spend a lot more time and they’ve given me a lot more work. Yeah, I have to give everything – especially oh I was so upset about (?) – I didn’t know what I was doing then.

Interviewer:	Have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

Subject:	Yes we have, yeah. I’ve only come across one female lecturer – yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think the female lecturer has a different style of teaching to the male lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, not really – similar.

Interviewer:	Do you find it encouraging to have a female lecturer?

Subject:	Erm, yes, it is for the girls in here, yes, so you can look at her like thinking that if she can do it, I can do that kind of thing that you get

Interviewer:	Would you like to see more females and have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, it would be good, yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Yes, I think so, yes.

Interviewer:	And do those lecturers treat the female and male students the same?

Subject:	Hmm, yes, yes, so far.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Er yes.

Interviewer:	Is that a male or female?

Subject:	Male.

Interviewer:	Have you had to go to him for anything at all?

Subject:	Erm, not really apart from well, er we shouldn’t – he expected to see him after exams (OK), when the result comes out and other than that we just sometimes walk by, and pop in – are you still alive? You know, that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that your personal tutor is approachable if you had to go to them with any problems?

Subject:	Oh yes, he’s very friendly and helpful, yes.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with your personal tutor or would you rather have had a female personal tutor?

Subject:	No, I don’t really mind yeah, he’s OK, yeah.

Interviewer:	Who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

Subject:	Er, biggest influence. I think it’s my friends in the class – yes. If I see them do well it’s – it isn’t that kind of competition you feel – it’s like – if they can do it, I can do it as well. You know it’s encouraging to see – you know – some people around. You know how friends influence you – yeah? That yeah – yeah, that kind of influence, not like competition between friends, yeah.

Interviewer:	But they support you? (yeah) Have you had to do much group work or presentation work as part of your course?

Subject:	Yes, we do quite a few group work. Not that many presentations but a lot of team projects.

Interviewer:	And when you’re doing group work, do you get put into groups or can you choose who you want to work with?

Subject:	Er, in year 1 we tend to be put into groups and in year 2 I think, yeah, so far we’ve been choosing our own group mates.

Interviewer:	And how do you decide who you want to work with in the group?

Subject:	I – well, I’ve been working with my friends, yeah, but I was also thinking of working with other people, on the course, who were sort of like expecting me to be in the group, so I just got shepherd (lost words) – yeah, ‘cos I don’t know – I am – in a way I used to being looked after all the time, and my friends are really – I’m really lucky to have them. They are really caring and they look after me as well and yeah, erm, I – I can’t deny that they’re doing a lot better than I am – but they don’t look down on me or anything, they help as much as they can, that’s why I wanted to do a project without them, so I can be in this like with other people and I can use my full strengths – yeah.

Interviewer:	And have you found, in the group, men or women are better to work with or doesn’t it matter?

Subject:	Erm, I – mm, it could be good to have a girl or (pause) – it is more or less the same.

Interviewer:	That’s alright. Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, a bit yeah. I think – I think it’s just the personality and you know of a particular person here and he – that person was so dominant, he had to be in charge of everything. I sort of really don’t like that, yeah, don’t like his – he’s like he’s on toy you, so – have I been through worst times? Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the men tend to take on that dominant role more often than women?

Subject:	Oh yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	Was he like it with the men within the group or was he like it just with the women?

Subject:	No, he was just like that to everybody. Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, well what part of the university course and the teaching advice do you think will help you on your placement?

Subject:	Er, what part? I’m not …

Interviewer:	Don’t you think there’s any particular skills that you’ve learnt that’ll help you?

Subject:	Yeah – I think pretty much everything we’ve been learning so far – yeah. Sort of expecting you – like reinforce my study when on a placement (yes) and then I’ve been told it’s kind of different.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s not just the technical things but the things like doing group work and working with other people – that will help you?

Subject:	Oh yeah, definitely I should think, yeah, because you can’t always work with people you like, yeah all the time, yeah.

Interviewer:	And do you think that there’ll be any skills that you can take from the part time work you’ve done?

Subject:	Er, (pause) I think it’s those interpersonal skills, yeah, communication and things with other member of staff, yeah – yeah pretty much the same. Sometimes a bit of pressure on – yeah.

Interviewer:	Has the university done anything to help you prepare for your placement, do you think?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, they – they do, ‘cos our tutor tried to find as many employers as he could and information regarding the employer or the opportunities – right. And, er, it’s OK that – not as extensive as I’d heard, from other departments – they’re sort of like looking for placement on behalf of a student – the student. I tell them that I think it’s a good idea that we have to be so active and involved in terms of looking for placement. So, it’s kind of another experience of how, you know, you look for a job. I think, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that being on an engineering course, and the type of teaching you’ve had, the whole experience really – do you think that reflects what it’ll be like when you get into the industry?

Subject:	From what I heard, no. I’ve not thought about it until I had an interview with employers. I’ve never had any first hand information from employers and it could be different, yeah, because there’s so many people and people from different like – different areas you have to deal with. So it is different – it’s in university you’d be treated the same but – I would expect different in industry, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think the classes in university could help you prepare for that kind of thing by telling you what it might be like. Do you think that’d help or…?

Subject:	Mm, it’s worth mentioning that – I think most of the female in the engineering, before they go into industry they – well I do, I’ve come expecting, you know. You bound to, you know, get something up there – some of the situations until you’re working wise – yeah, I would expect it.

Interviewer:	OK, did anyone particularly encourage you, or try to discourage you from going on the placement?

Subject:	No – no but – well I mean I haven’t had anyone disencourage me from going on placement. On the – most of the people who’ve been on, they keep saying it’s a fantastic experience, so encouraging me.

Interviewer:	Do you know where you’re going on placement yet?

Subject:	I don’t know – anywhere I’m asked (laughter)

Interviewer:	Have you applied and are waiting to hear from companies, at the minute?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m waiting, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, the companies that you have applied to, how did you decide to apply to those particular companies?

Subject:	Er, how? Erm, a lot of the profile – erm I tend to apply to some companies with a large scale project, rather than just say probably doing a bit of maintenance and that kind of thing, yeah. (lost words) probably not the biggest. I personally don’t really want to go for the biggest international crew for my placement. ‘cos I do that – it’s just like a tiny fish in a big pond – that kind of thing. Erm, it could be in terms of responsibility you will be given less, in a big company because everything – I would expect it’s so systematic you would be given a specific type of running of it all, yeah. So I go for like medium size.

Interviewer:	OK, did you look at anything like pay or equal opportunities, or travelling opportunities that companies might give you?

Subject:	Yeah, looking at them – I didn’t – I don’t really look at the pay ‘cos I expect them similar than you do on placement year, and erm I haven’t looked at equal opportunities and stuff but they all have like a line of say equal you know opportunity employer and erm, I would expect they deal with, that sometimes it’s not their control, they have a particular like, I don’t know – kind of mind, you know, male employee in the office, yeah. I look at the, training or for me I’m looking at if like – sometimes they will say if you perform well on your placement you might get a choice here – not a scholarship, sponsorship, you know, for your final year or you might be given job when you finish here, that kind of thing. I look at that as well, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, where did you go to find out the information about the companies?

Subject:	Er, I’ve used erm Dr Job, on the internet and that it’s very helpful and there’s another one called – I think it’s Hobsons – yeah, where they issue a lot of them brochures. They’re very useful, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, I think we said a bit already about the university helping you find the placement, but do you think that they did help you or would you have liked more help or less help?

Subject:	Erm, I think it’s about I’d say, level now, they don’t help too much. It’s the whole process, I think doing occasionally - it’s just not – the experience you’ve gained when you’re actually in the company, the whole process you start preparing, looking at company profiles, you know, and deciding who to apply and the application process and you have to talk to strangers and you are waiting for reply and so on, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do things like that help you when you…?

Subject:	Yes, definitely, definitely, yeah,

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of skills and experience are you expecting to get from your placement?

Subject:	I would expect a lot of communication skills (yeah) yeah, a lot of it and well from what I’ve been told mainly what – you know, the biggest part you get out of – erm, they were saying you may be expecting, you know, things quite different from what you’ve been learning. You know, that kind of thing. Yeah – interpersonal skills, and yeah, communication and I think that would be what I get out of it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll have much opportunity to put the theory that you’ve learnt into practice, or …?

Subject:	Yeah, I think there’s bound to be some opportunities to put theory into practice. Like, if I go on er go an do contracting, I would imagine working in – spending more time on site, you know, doing a lot of levelling, some site surveying – that sort of thing. And we’ve been learning surveying in year 1 and year 2 – this is our 2nd module so far. And all the basic knowledge of the instrument and yeah, I think it would be useful.

Interviewer:	What do you think will be the worse thing about going on placement?

Subject:	The worse thing? It could be hard, you know, trying to dig up all your memories – you know after a year. You have to take up, like your (map?) and the materials on the course, you know. Up – before that – but then I think, so many have people have been on it, it should be OK, otherwise you know, people will be saying it would be worse going off from here, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, and what about the best thing – what do you think will be the best thing?

Subject:	The best thing? Er, for me because I haven’t really been in industry or any site – a normal, professional like job, I’ve only been working in shops or in restaurants, things like that. It will be really good experience to see really how a proper job feels – yeah.

Interviewer:	What sort of work do you want to be doing when you’re on the placement? Is it site work that you’d like to do?

Subject:	Erm, well, I wanted to do a bit of both to start with. Erm, I personally prefer doing design stuff in the office. Personally I prefer a consultants to a contractor (period?) but er, I don’t have strong preference at this moment.

Interviewer:	Have you applied to both sort of companies?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the placement will help make your mind up about what you want to do when you finish?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely because if I want to enter like – you know, consultants aren’t quite – and then I find out, because I think it has to be one or another – yeah? And, if I find out this is not suitable for me, so I’d better, you know, start thinking of contracting and vice versa, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	Being at work – hmm, I think erm, more pressurised in terms of meeting deadline and things, ‘cos at university if you don’t do your piece of coursework, it’s your own responsibility – no-one else will hurt, but if you can’t do that or you can’t feel like – oh, I don’t feel like obviously work this morning – that kind of stuff. Yeah, it’s the responsibility I think and a lot of pressure. It just depends on how you feel and how you take the balance, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that in some ways, the course that you’ve done will help for that, because you’ve said that your degree is a more pressurised course?

Subject:	Well, I think – well, with having so many coursework and deadline, almost every other week, I think it will definitely help because we all know that if we don’t a meet a deadline or we don’t say do our work, it’s not worth us, you know, staying on the course. Yeah – so…

Interviewer:	That’s good. In terms of your career, where do you see yourself in 5 years time.

Subject:	In 5 years time? Erm, if I doing say (pause) decide to go in consultant work – could be erm, a – a leader in a design team, or if I work on site could be project manager, yeah.

Interviewer:	You’d like to go into the management side of type things then?

Subject:	Er, (pause) Project Manager, I think from what I’ve been learning so far is to – because if you have been long enough in industry, you’d be stuck, you know, running the project rather than doing the actual duty and yeah, that’s it.

Interviewer:	OK, what about in 10 years time?

Subject:	10 years? (laughs) I could be housewife. Erm, no, er …

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will stay in the engineering industry?

Subject:	Yeah, I think I would do. I talking from this stage, yeah. Erm, I would do, I think, yeah. Still in the same industry which hopefully is higher in company, rather than like another engineer, yeah.

Interviewer:	You’re probably joking about being a housewife, but do you think that if you do get married and have children that will be compatible with working in engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I’ve really thought about it, to be honest. I think it’s really difficult that you have to just – and decide yourself. To me, I have sort of like a fair idea. I’ll definitely work for another 3 or 5 years before I will get married or think about children, and once I have children – ‘cos for that length of year, I’ve already established and, you know, reputation or I don’t know, experience – mm, I probably would thinking if I was married, at that stage, I probably thinking of having my own children. I’ll probably leave for a couple of years til they, you know, get a bit older, yeah, first – yeah, that’s what I plan.

Interviewer:	No, that’s fine. Do you think that because you’re in a male industry, that if you’ve got children, then you might get treated differently?

Subject:	Erm, if they don’t – I think they won’t treat you differently because you have children, it’s because you have children and starting to effect, you know, team work or things like that – they will look at you differently, yes.

Interviewer:	OK, what would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Ideal career? Erm, I don’t know, just enjoy what I do, not do it for the sake of money. Of course money’s important but I would like a job that I really enjoy not just because I have – I need money.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you’ll come across any problems partly to get what you want, in terms of that?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know – it shouldn’t be a problem because – although, I did find civil engineering hard, that I do enjoy what I do, at the moment and I’ll probably carry on enjoying it.

Interviewer:	OK, would you like to go and work abroad at all?

Subject:	I would, yeah. I would. Considering that – any opportunity that suits me, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are quite good in civil engineering at the minute?

Subject:	Er, yeah, yeah. Erm, hard to say really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that once you get in the industry, you’ve said in 10 years time you’d like to do civil engineering, but higher up, do you think that the opportunities will be there?

Subject:	Yeah, if you perform well and you do a good job. It’s – I think, or – I don’t think it’s just civil engineering, it’s so realistic in any type of career. If you work well, people will know and you get promoted and you have more and more responsibility and authority, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, are you pleased with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

Subject:	Erm, yes.

Interviewer:	Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again? Would you (refuse?) going straight to an engineering degree instead of having started in chemistry?

Subject:	Yeah, I think I would. Straight engineering is – I really wanted having – I really wanted to have a career related to my study, otherwise in a way I would think is this a waste of 3 years? Yeah.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	Hard work, a lot of hard work and long hours as well, yes.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the engineering culture is male and masculine?

Subject:	Pardon?

Interviewer:	Do you think that the engineering culture is male?

Subject:	Erm, it is how it is now, but I don’t think it should be the way it is now, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any part of the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

Subject:	Any part?

Interviewer:	Do you think that any part of the engineering culture will cause any problems?

Subject:	Yeah, it could be. I think probably that most of the problems arise on site because you get so many different people, especially the workmen. You know what they’re like. They think a building should be male work. No woman should be allowed on the site, you know, that kind of thing. You do get one of these people about somewhere and I don’t think you – you’ll have any other problems.

Interviewer:	If you are working on site, how do you think that you’ll deal with that?

Subject:	Er, well you just have to be stronger. You can’t be soft, because they will just – you know – choose people to pick on – victims, if they know you. And I think, if you’re doing your work well and you show your ability and you have more respect and things will get better, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it helps or it could help if you’re more like one of the lads and male or feminine?

Subject:	It could be worth, having like more of a boyish kind of attitude, but not to want to be a man, you know, yeah. More open-minded and, yeah, probably less feminine on site, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the engineering industry will stay male dominated or do you think that more females will go into the industry and improve the situation?

Subject:	It will change but I imagine it’s very slowly. Probably compared of 10 years, you know, before, the number of female engineers have improved a great deal but still the proportion’s so tiny. So I would imagine it will get better but very slowly, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s all the questions I have. Thanks very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you get the train then?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.text: OK, when you decided to do engineering, did you realise it was so male-dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject

I – yes, so I don’t see any reason why not. If you enjoy maths and science then – those subjects, I don’t see why not, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think there aren’t more women in engineering then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think just traditions. Erm, but yeah that’s about it, I think and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think that more women could be encouraged to do engineering then?

turns.text: Well, I think to start with er I think some kind of education or some talk could be good in like primary or – not – primary’s probably too young – secondary schools.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, people could go in and tell them what…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah tell them – well specially tell the girls – could tell the boys as well - remind the girls it’s not just a boys’ subject, you know, that kind of thing. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, characteristic – I’m not sure ‘cos – well it’s very general I think you have to have this characteristic and also – ‘cos also if you want to do the choice in your career well – but civil engineering it’s probably – the workload, its much heavier than others – I don’t know because I haven’t done, you know, any other areas yet. Erm,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think people doing chemistry and people doing civil engineering have different characteristics then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well really I do, yeah. Erm doing – people doing like civil engineering, they’re very determined. They’re very determined in terms of where they want to end up being, like a few years or really what they want to do. Erm, yeah, erm quite strong minded and I think more ambitious as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there’s a difference between women engineers and men engineers? Do you think they have different characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, could be. Not – yeah, but probably for men it’s just – yeah, one of the area I can succeed in, you know, that kind of thing. I could be wrong but I – I do feel that there is something like competition between female and the male in this – in the same industry. But being civil engineering, it’s so dominated by males. The female would think, if you can do it why can’t I do it? You know that kind of feeling.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you think that’s why the women are more ambitious probably? (yeah, yeah) Because they have to prove that basically?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of being a female engineer?

Yeah.

turns.text: It is?

turns.text: Yeah.

turns.text: Do you think that your personal tutor is approachable if you had to go to them with any problems?

turns.text: But they support you? (yeah) Have you had to do much group work or presentation work as part of your course?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And have you found, in the group, men or women are better to work with or doesn’t it matter?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I – mm, it could be good to have a girl or (pause) – it is more or less the same.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s alright. Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the men tend to take on that dominant role more often than women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah, yeah.

turns.text: Was he like it with the men within the group or was he like it just with the women?

turns.text: Do you think that’s not just the technical things but the things like doing group work and working with other people – that will help you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the university done anything to help you prepare for your placement, do you think?

turns.text: Erm, yeah, they – they do, ‘cos our tutor tried to find as many employers as he could and information regarding the employer or the opportunities – right. I think, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that being on an engineering course, and the type of teaching you’ve had, the whole experience really – do you think that reflects what it’ll be like when you get into the industry?

So it is different – it’s in university you’d be treated the same but – I would expect different in industry, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the classes in university could help you prepare for that kind of thing by telling you what it might be like. Do you think that’d help or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, it’s worth mentioning that – I think most of the female in the engineering, before they go into industry they – well I do, I’ve come expecting, you know. You bound to, you know, get something up there – some of the situations until you’re working wise – yeah, I would expect it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did anyone particularly encourage you, or try to discourage you from going on the placement?

turns.text: No – no but – well I mean I haven’t had anyone disencourage me from going on placement. On the – most of the people who’ve been on, they keep saying it’s a fantastic experience, so encouraging me.

turns.text: Do you know where you’re going on placement yet?

turns.text: I don’t know – anywhere I’m asked (laughter)

turns.text: Have you applied and are waiting to hear from companies, at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’m waiting, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, the companies that you have applied to, how did you decide to apply to those particular companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, how? (lost words) probably not the biggest. I personally don’t really want to go for the biggest international crew for my placement. ‘cos I do that – it’s just like a tiny fish in a big pond – that kind of thing. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you look at anything like pay or equal opportunities, or travelling opportunities that companies might give you?

turns.speaker: Subject

I look at the, training or for me I’m looking at if like – sometimes they will say if you perform well on your placement you might get a choice here – not a scholarship, sponsorship, you know, for your final year or you might be given job when you finish here, that kind of thing. I look at that as well, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, where did you go to find out the information about the companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I’ve used erm Dr Job, on the internet and that it’s very helpful and there’s another one called – I think it’s Hobsons – yeah, where they issue a lot of them brochures. They’re very useful, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I think we said a bit already about the university helping you find the placement, but do you think that they did help you or would you have liked more help or less help?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do things like that help you when you…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely, definitely, yeah,

turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the placement will help make your mind up about what you want to do when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely because if I want to enter like – you know, consultants aren’t quite – and then I find out, because I think it has to be one or another – yeah? And, if I find out this is not suitable for me, so I’d better, you know, start thinking of contracting and vice versa, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Being at work – hmm, I think erm, more pressurised in terms of meeting deadline and things, ‘cos at university if you don’t do your piece of coursework, it’s your own responsibility – no-one else will hurt, but if you can’t do that or you can’t feel like – oh, I don’t feel like obviously work this morning – that kind of stuff. Yeah, it’s the responsibility I think and a lot of pressure. It just depends on how you feel and how you take the balance, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that in some ways, the course that you’ve done will help for that, because you’ve said that your degree is a more pressurised course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I think – well, with having so many coursework and deadline, almost every other week, I think it will definitely help because we all know that if we don’t a meet a deadline or we don’t say do our work, it’s not worth us, you know, staying on the course. Yeah – so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s good. In terms of your career, where do you see yourself in 5 years time.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In 5 years time? Erm, if I doing say (pause) decide to go in consultant work – could be erm, a – a leader in a design team, or if I work on site could be project manager, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’d like to go into the management side of type things then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, (pause) Project Manager, I think from what I’ve been learning so far is to – because if you have been long enough in industry, you’d be stuck, you know, running the project rather than doing the actual duty and yeah, that’s it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about in 10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 10 years? (laughs) I could be housewife. Erm, no, er …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you will stay in the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think I would do. I talking from this stage, yeah. Erm, I would do, I think, yeah. Still in the same industry which hopefully is higher in company, rather than like another engineer, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’re probably joking about being a housewife, but do you think that if you do get married and have children that will be compatible with working in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’ve really thought about it, to be honest. I think it’s really difficult that you have to just – and decide yourself. To me, I have sort of like a fair idea. I’ll definitely work for another 3 or 5 years before I will get married or think about children, and once I have children – ‘cos for that length of year, I’ve already established and, you know, reputation or I don’t know, experience – mm, I probably would thinking if I was married, at that stage, I probably thinking of having my own children. I’ll probably leave for a couple of years til they, you know, get a bit older, yeah, first – yeah, that’s what I plan.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No, that’s fine. Do you think that because you’re in a male industry, that if you’ve got children, then you might get treated differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, if they don’t – I think they won’t treat you differently because you have children, it’s because you have children and starting to effect, you know, team work or things like that – they will look at you differently, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ideal career? Erm, I don’t know, just enjoy what I do, not do it for the sake of money. Of course money’s important but I would like a job that I really enjoy not just because I have – I need money.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you’ll come across any problems partly to get what you want, in terms of that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know – it shouldn’t be a problem because – although, I did find civil engineering hard, that I do enjoy what I do, at the moment and I’ll probably carry on enjoying it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you like to go and work abroad at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would, yeah. I would. Considering that – any opportunity that suits me, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are quite good in civil engineering at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah, yeah. Erm, hard to say really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that once you get in the industry, you’ve said in 10 years time you’d like to do civil engineering, but higher up, do you think that the opportunities will be there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, if you perform well and you do a good job. It’s – I think, or – I don’t think it’s just civil engineering, it’s so realistic in any type of career. If you work well, people will know and you get promoted and you have more and more responsibility and authority, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you pleased with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again? Would you (refuse?) going straight to an engineering degree instead of having started in chemistry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think I would. Straight engineering is – I really wanted having – I really wanted to have a career related to my study, otherwise in a way I would think is this a waste of 3 years? Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hard work, a lot of hard work and long hours as well, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the engineering culture is male and masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Pardon?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the engineering culture is male?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it is how it is now, but I don’t think it should be the way it is now, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any part of the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Any part?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any part of the engineering culture will cause any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it could be. I think probably that most of the problems arise on site because you get so many different people, especially the workmen. You know what they’re like. They think a building should be male work. No woman should be allowed on the site, you know, that kind of thing. You do get one of these people about somewhere and I don’t think you – you’ll have any other problems.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you are working on site, how do you think that you’ll deal with that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, well you just have to be stronger. You can’t be soft, because they will just – you know – choose people to pick on – victims, if they know you. And I think, if you’re doing your work well and you show your ability and you have more respect and things will get better, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it helps or it could help if you’re more like one of the lads and male or feminine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It could be worth, having like more of a boyish kind of attitude, but not to want to be a man, you know, yeah. More open-minded and, yeah, probably less feminine on site, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the engineering industry will stay male dominated or do you think that more females will go into the industry and improve the situation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It will change but I imagine it’s very slowly. Probably compared of 10 years, you know, before, the number of female engineers have improved a great deal but still the proportion’s so tiny. So I would imagine it will get better but very slowly, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s all the questions I have. Thanks very much.
